Changelog

Source: NEWS.md

npnormalize 0.1.9

The signature does not move. np_normalize_signature() still reports v1-5e901add4a04a5d6, so nothing cached under 0.1.8 needs rebuilding. This release adds one function.

np_signature_history() dates a signature

A signature is opaque by design — that is what makes it a good fingerprint and a poor label. Until now the record of which release produced which value was prose: a comment beside the pin in tests/testthat/test-signature.R, which a person can read and a script cannot.

That cost something real. Consumers stamp provenance headers from packageVersion(), which dates the current signature and is no help for a historical one, so matchdb and pfmatch each dated v1-59c6e84c5f38e9f5 by hand out of NEWS.md — an inference sitting in a header that is supposed to carry a record.

np_signature_history(np_normalize_signature())
#>             signature     package version                              summary
#> 1 v1-5e901add4a04a5d6 npnormalize   0.1.8 the join stops closing up a lone ...

version is the release that introduced the signature, so one signature is one row and the column stays comparable; a later release reporting the same value unchanged is named in summary instead of getting a row of its own, which is the case for 0.1.1 and for this release.

The three oldest rows are npmatch’s, from before the normalizer moved into this package. They are listed rather than omitted so that an unrecognized value can be told from a recognized pre-split one — np_signature_history() on an unknown signature returns no rows, which is a different answer from a listed row whose version is NA. Their npmatch version was never written down anywhere findable, so version is NA and summary says where the value is cited: v1-421e1e2a6afb024e in pfmatch’s dev/BASELINE-2026-08 and matchdb’s dev/GROUP-STRUCTURE-FINDINGS.md, v1-6dcb298522cc5118 as npmatch@ddfd967, v1-b42811fe6601afe6 in matchdb’s dev/verify/build-baseline-2026-10.R. Undated, not guessed.

A test asserts the installed signature appears in the table with a version at or behind the installed one, so adding a release without adding its row fails rather than drifting. It uses utils::compareVersion() rather than a string comparison, because "0.1.10" sorts before "0.1.8" lexically and would fail a correct install on the first double-digit patch — a trap pointed out by a pfmatch reviewer who had just hit it in their own normalizer gate.

Asked for by matchdb and pfmatch, which both needed to write the version beside the signature without a human looking it up. # npnormalize 0.1.8

One correction to 0.1.7, found by measuring what 0.1.7’s house-number join did to matchdb’s 22,026,817-row address table before adopting it there. The join is a clear gain — isolated from the other three releases in the same signature move, it merges 7,583 EIN-level address groups — but it was closing up a hyphen in one place it should not.

A lone compass letter is a direction, not part of the house number (#16)

In 70-11 150TH STREET the hyphen is structural, and closing it up is the whole point of #16. In 1002-E SENECA ST the hyphen is a typed-over space in front of a direction, and closing it up invented a house number:

street 0.1.7 street_key 0.1.8 street_key
1002 - E SENECA STREET 1002E SENECA ST 1002 E SENECA ST
1002 E SENECA ST 1002 E SENECA ST 1002 E SENECA ST
1013- N 5TH ST 1013N 5TH ST 1013 N 5TH ST
10-S 462 CARRINGTON CIRCLE 10S 462 CARRINGTON CIR 10 S 462 CARRINGTON CIR

1002E is not a door, and the key no longer met the spelling of the same door filed with a space — the split #16 set out to close, reintroduced one row over.

.np_hyphen_house now excludes N, S, E and W where they stand alone, and only there: 123-A MAIN ST is a lettered house number and still joins, because A is not a compass point. A spelled-out direction was never a single letter to the join, so 123-EAST MAIN ST was already left alone. The cost is a unit letter that happens to be a compass point (123-E meaning unit E), which is spaced instead — which is what 0.1.6 did to every lettered house number.

To be clear about what this does not fix: every other lettered house number still keys apart from its spaced spelling. 875-A ISLAND DRIVE reaches 875A ISLAND DR and 875 A ISLAND DRIVE reaches 875 A ISLAND DR, as do 57-C and 1801-C. That is the ordinary and larger case; the carve-out only moves N, S, E and W out of it, because a compass letter is the one whose spaced spelling is certainly the same address.

Measured over matchdb’s address table: 459 strings move, closing 39 of the join’s 1,496 EIN-level address splits.

The splits the join still leaves, and why

The same measurement found what #16’s adoption note could not: the join merges 7,583 address groups and splits 1,496.

Two counts appear below and they are not the same population. 1,496 is the join’s own, isolated by re-deriving every affected street with and without .np_join_house_number(); it is the figure to cite for what this rule does. 1,499 is what the 0.1.3 → 0.1.8 diff reported, which carries four releases, and it is the set the classification below was run over. The difference is the other releases, not uncertainty about the join.

Those splits were then classified over the 1,499 the diff reported, and not one of them differs in anything beyond its separators: 505 are the same raw string once every mark is stripped, and in the other 994 the two keys agree once their spaces are. That is a test on strings, not a reading of addresses, and for 20 of the 1,499 it does not settle which street — 1049-38 STREET against 1049 38 ST STE 400 could be a house number on an unnamed numeric street or a house number on a numbered one, and nothing in either string says which. street_num is no help: it disagrees across all 1,499, which is what the join does to it by design.

the three spellings of one Queens door 0.1.3 key 0.1.8 key
100-09 METROPOLITAN AVENUE 100 09 METROPOLITAN AVE 10009 METROPOLITAN AVE
100 09 METROPOLITAN AVE 100 09 METROPOLITAN AVE 100 09 METROPOLITAN AVE
10009 METROPOLITAN AVE 10009 METROPOLITAN AVE 10009 METROPOLITAN AVE

0.1.3 grouped the first two and 0.1.8 groups the last two; no rule groups all three, because a space-separated run cannot be told from a house number followed by a numeric street name. 27 41 HORSENECK RD is house 27-41; 120 66 ST is house 120 on 66 St; nothing in either string says which. The same holds for a letter: 101 B FOREST DR is house 101B, and 101 B ST is house 101 on B Street.

Joining the spaced spelling as well was measured over the same table, under the same compass-letter exclusion. It looks good in the aggregate and is wrong in the particular: measured over one set of strings it closes 1,156 of the splits and adds 2,650 merges, but it moves 92,797 further strings, and the strings it moves are street names.

street with the spaced join what the street is
5001 11 MILE RD 500111 MILE RD 11 Mile Road, Michigan
712 H STREET NE 712H ST NE H Street NE, Washington DC
17398 M 86 17398M86 M-86, a Michigan state highway
964 60 RD 96460 RD 60 Road, a Colorado grid road
1801 C ST 1801C ST C Street
15039 4H CENTER LN 150394H CENTER LN 4-H Center Lane

17,614 of those 92,797 are a house number followed by a bare numeric or single-letter street name, which is the shape the rule cannot tell from a hyphenated house number; the rest include the cases above. So the merges it adds are not all real.

The blunter version of the idea now argues less strongly against itself, and that is worth saying plainly. pfmatch measured a full space strip — gsub(" ", "", street_key) — under 0.1.6 and found 2,278 merges of which 972 (42.67%) joined rows whose street_num disagreed. Re-measured under this signature, the same script over the same 3,880,431-row reference gives 1,886 merges with 322 (17.07%) disagreeing, because the house-number join had already done part of that key’s work on the hyphenated spellings (pfmatch dev/ADDR-KEY-SPELLINGS-20261102.log). 1,886 with 322 suspect is a better trade than 2,278 with 972, so that figure no longer carries the rejection: it says a blanket space strip is less bad than it was, not that it is safe. What carries the rejection is the 92,797 strings above, measured over 22,026,817 rows, which is a kind of evidence a 3.88M-row reference cannot produce.

The 1,457 splits that remain are therefore deliberate: 0.0066% of the address table, against 7,566 merges, and the alternative is worse.

There is no consumer-side escape hatch, and an earlier draft of this note wrongly offered one. It said a consumer who would rather have the merges could key on street_num, “now the whole number on both spellings”. It is not: it is the whole number on the hyphenated spelling only, which is what the join is for.

street street_key street_num
70-11 150TH STREET 7011 150TH ST 7011
70 11 150TH STREET 70 11 150TH ST 70
875-A ISLAND DRIVE 875A ISLAND DR 875A
875 A ISLAND DRIVE 875 A ISLAND DR 875

So keying on street_num reproduces the split rather than closing it, for every one of the ~1,500. It merges the hyphenated spelling with the closed-up one, which street_key already does. Reported by a pfmatch reviewer who probed the suggestion instead of taking it. # npnormalize 0.1.7

Two spelling problems, one on each side of the frame, both of them a case where the normalizer split one thing into two keys. Neither was a typo class: a hyphenated house number is how whole jurisdictions write an address, and a word broken across two tokens is a fixed-width line break in the filing.

A hyphen in a house number is closed up rather than spaced (#16)

.np_basic_clean() turns every mark into a space, which is right for a name and wrong for a house number. 70-11 150TH STREET keyed as 70 11 150TH ST while 7011 150TH STREET — the same Queens door, filed the other way — keyed as 7011 150TH ST, so the two never blocked together and np_addr_key() put them in different groups. It cost two more columns on the way: street_num was truncated to 70, and street_name absorbed the remainder as 11 150TH, which is wrong rather than merely short.

.np_join_house_number() closes the hyphen up before the clean runs, so all three columns are right at once:

street street_key street_num street_name
70-11 150TH STREET 7011 150TH ST 7011 150TH
7011 150TH STREET 7011 150TH ST 7011 150TH
73-4460 QUEEN KAAHUMANU HWY 734460 QUEEN KAAHUMANU HWY 734460 QUEEN KAAHUMANU
123-A MAIN ST 123A MAIN ST 123A MAIN

Three conventions, not three mistakes: Queens block-and-house numbers (70-11 is block 70, house 11), Hawaii’s prefix numbers, and Chicago-style ranges. Over the 3,687,435-row unified BMF, 6,642 rows (0.180%) carry such a number and every one of their keys moves. Counting address groups that hold both spellings of one address (street_key + zip5), 87 before and 293 after — 206 groups that were two.

Closing the hyphen up, rather than keeping it, is the choice that makes the two filed spellings one key, which is what a street key is for. A Chicago range fuses as a side effect (5830-5832 becomes 58305832), which is no better a house number than the 5830 it used to truncate to but no worse, and its street_name is now right. There is a test asserting that, so it reads as a decision rather than a surprise.

The join is anchored and narrow on purpose. Only a leading house number is joined, so HC 81 BOX 363-5 and PO BOX 363-5 keep their separator and the box vocabulary is untouched; and the part after the hyphen must be digits or a single letter, so 123-MAIN ST cannot be glued into one token. It runs after the unit strip, which means a hyphenated number behind a unit is still found — PMB 125 3434-135 KILDAIRE FARM RD joins once PMB 125 is gone — and a chain joins whole, so 38-39-205 ST gives 3839205 ST.

Fixing it here rather than in each consumer was #16’s own measurement: keying on gsub(" ", "", street_key) adds 2,278 merges over a comparable reference, of which 972 (42.67%) join rows whose street_num disagrees — 4780 1 55 N with 47801 55 N — while only 410 are this case.

Eleven more spellings of FOUNDATION, and the one that stays (#17)

0.1.6 folded FDN, FND, FNDTN and FDTN. .np_abbrev now also takes FOUNDATIO, FOUNDATI, FOUNDATON, FOUNDATN, FOUNDTN, FOUNDATOIN, FOUNDAITON, FOUNDATIION, FOUDATION and FOUNATION, and the new .np_split_words rejoins the three forms where a line break fell inside the word — FOUND ATION, FOUNDATIO N, FOUNDATI ON. 1,182 EINs, every one of whose name_key moves, and name_form now reports FOUNDATION for them instead of nothing.

The rejoin runs before the abbreviation table, and the order is load-bearing: run .np_abbrev first and FOUNDATIO N becomes FOUNDATION N, a key no correctly spelled row has. np_name_rules() gains a split_words element so a port in another engine gets both tables and the ordering is stated where a porter will read it.

ROCKY MOUNTAIN ELK FOUNATION now keys to ROCKY MOUNTAIN ELK, which 747 other EINs already share. That is the intended behaviour and not a false merge: FOUNDATION is stripped from name_key for the correctly spelled siblings too, name_key is a blocking key rather than an identity, and name_core is the column that keeps the word. The defect was that these rows sat outside a block their own siblings were in.

FOUND is deliberately not folded, for the reason PHYS is not. It is an English word. Of the BMF rows whose name ends in FOUND, the ones that would gain a blocking partner are mostly not truncations — LOST AND FOUND, PRO FOUND, BE FOUND, HOPE FOUND, FOREVER FOUND — and folding them mis-blocks a thrift shop, a ministry and a theatre for the sake of roughly ten genuine cases such as AMERICAN UNIVERSITY OF PARIS FOUND. Position does not separate the two readings either: ANGEL FOUND FOR ANIMALS is the word mid-name and ASSOC FOUND OF ROCHESTER NY the abbreviation mid-name. The decision is recorded in a test and in the comment beside the table, so the next reader does not add it blind.

One hand-copy closed on the way

np_normalize() and the dba_key / division_key lines each inlined .np_replace_tokens(.np_basic_clean(x), .np_abbrev), so the sequence existed in four places and .np_clean_name() — which exists to be that sequence — was reached only by np_name_core() and np_name_placeholder(). Adding the rejoin to four copies is the same hand-copy problem the box vocabulary had, so the call sites go through .np_clean_name() now. No behaviour change of its own.

The signature

This moves np_normalize_signature() to v1-59c6e84c5f38e9f5. street_key, street_num, street_name, name_key, name_full, name_form, dba_key and division_key can all change, so stored keys and every statistic built on them must be rebuilt — matchdb’s derived tables, bundles and tranches, and pfmatch::pf_variants.

Measured against 0.1.6 on a fixed 400,000-row sample, with both versions run over the same rows rather than against the stored columns: 734 street keys and 131 name keys move, and every one of them is one of these two fixes. On the 399,140 rows neither fix touches, name_full, name_form, street_num and street_name are identical. The handful of moved rows that fell outside the crude detection patterns used for that check were all the fixes working on inputs the patterns did not anticipate — a hyphen chain, a hyphenated number behind a unit, and FOUND- ATION.

npnormalize 0.1.6

The policy question behind #13, answered family by family, and the signal a blanked box was throwing away. np_addr_key() answers same building?, so every mail-delivery address has to be blank in it — leaving one in does not add a wrong row, it builds a cluster, because every box-holder in a ZIP becomes a co-tenant of every other and the address-sharing statistics then read that crowd as an office building. Four families were measured against that rule and two of them keep their key.

The box vocabulary takes the spellings #13 measured

.np_box_head gains PO BX, PB and PB BOX, P BOX and its zero-for-the-O typo P B0X, POSTAL OFC BOX, APDO, and the DRAWER family (bare, or behind PO / POST OFC / POSTAL). Over the 3,687,435-row unified BMF that is 58 more rows detected and 0 lost, in 54 keys, every one of which is a box a filer spelled unusually.

The identifier had to move with it. .np_box_identifier() read the first digit run in the whole key, which was correct only while no designator contained a digit — P B0X 102 took the 0 out of B0X and keyed all four of those rows to PO BOX 0, which is the lettered-box collapse of #12 in a new place: two different boxes landing on one address. The digits are now read from what follows the designator, still anywhere after it, because a box number is routinely followed by more text (PO BOX 102175 KOOSER RD). Corpus-wide the identifier moved on 0 rows that 0.1.5 already called boxes.

Measured and declined, so the decision is on the record rather than the spelling being missed: a bare BX (1 row), the unabbreviated APARTADO and BUZON (7), and CALLER BOX (1). APARTADO is the unabbreviated form of the APDO that was adopted, so it is the first candidate if this is revisited.

is_mail_only, a second gate on the address key

A new column and a new pattern for the designators that have no building and no identifier to compare: GENERAL DELIVERY and GEN DEL (158 rows), military mail — PSC 236, CMR 63, APO 12, FPO 7, DPO 0 — and the university mail drawers named by two letters (DRAWER AA UNIVERSITY OF MONTEVALLO, 20 rows). 496 rows that is_po_box cannot see.

GENERAL DELIVERY is the clearest case in the corpus: 117 rows whose street is that exact string and nothing else, so the key was GENERAL DELIVERY <zip> and every general-delivery filer in a ZIP was counted as one building’s tenants.

Two things it deliberately does not do. The street key is not rewritten — there is no box number to rewrite it to, and the string is the only thing the row says — and the flag is reported disjoint from is_po_box, so the two partition the buildingless addresses rather than overlapping on the drawers. A DRAWER sits in both vocabularies because DRAWER B has a comparable identifier and DRAWER JJ EMORY UNIVERSITY does not, and a caller should not have to know that. The address-key blank is the union either way, which is why np_pattern("mailonly") hands out the raw pattern: a SQL copy ORs the two and lands in the same place.

Anchored at ^ with a word boundary and no identifier, none of these reaches a street: 0 of the 3,998 rural-route keys, 0 BIN, 0 of the BOX ELDER / BOX SPGS family, and GEN DELANEY ST is safe because \b cannot run into a street name. The one row it takes from a KEEP family is APO MAILBOX 637 REED UN BLDG, which is an APO address.

What keeps its address key, and why

A rural route does, on the reasoning that it is unlike a box: it is a unique delivery point, so two filers at RR 1 BOX 8 in one ZIP really are at one place. #13 worried that routes would crowd instead; measured, they do not. Across 4,606 route-with-box address keys the most crowded holds 5 EINs, and across 570 bare-route keys, 2. The street_num collision #13 raised is real — RR 1 parses street_num 1 — but with clusters that size it has nothing to amplify.

A MAILBOX (123 rows) and a BIN (24) do too: both sit at a real street address, which the key keeps. BIN also still has a visible false positive at its volume, 1206 GRAIN BIN RD.

Together the two gates blank 581,166 of 3,687,435 rows, 554 more than 0.1.5. The address key is un-blanked on 0 rows and otherwise unchanged on 0, and the distinct address-key count falls by 538.

mail_key: what a blanked box still tells you

Blanking a box says two filers are not in one building. That is true, and it is all it says — but two organizations collecting mail from the same box are very likely administered by the same people, which is a different claim and a useful one. mail_key is the complement of the address key and carries it: the box and its ZIP ("PO BOX 1234 59801"), blank for everything else, including the mail-only designators, because GENERAL DELIVERY 59801 would rebuild exactly the false crowd the blank just removed.

It is idempotent on a rewritten street_key, which matters because matchdb caches that column and may hand back either form: POB 25161, P O 25161 and PO BOX 25161 all key to PO BOX 25161 <zip>. Corpus-wide 213 mail keys are built from more than one street key and every one is the same box spelled differently.

The count is not optional. 580,670 box rows fall into 496,830 mail keys, 7.43% of them shared by two or more EINs, and 20.79% of box-holding EINs sit on a shared box. But the populations at either end want opposite treatment: 30,097 of the 36,910 shared boxes hold exactly two EINs and 3,829 hold three — an organization and its foundation, a parent and its chapter — while 678 hold ten or more and the most crowded, PO BOX 653067 in ZIP 75265, holds 3,626. That is a service bureau, and reading it as common administration would link 3,626 unrelated organizations to each other. np_mail_freq() is the counterpart to np_addr_freq()’s share_min for exactly this, and its documentation carries the numbers.

Published for consumers

  • np_is_mail_only() joins np_is_po_box() and np_has_box() for a caller holding one free-text line.
  • np_mail_key() joins np_addr_key(); np_mail_freq() joins np_name_freq() and np_addr_freq().
  • np_pattern("mailonly") joins "pobox", "box" and "unit_id". test-portability.R now runs all four through R’s TRE and DuckDB’s RE2 over a 45-key fixture and asserts they agree, and it asserts two things a hand-ported SQL macro gets wrong: that a macro reading only "pobox" is narrower than np_addr_key(), and that the identifier is capture group 2 — the drawer alternative nests a group inside the head, and it has to stay non-capturing or group 2 silently becomes the drawer prefix.

Signature

This moves np_normalize_signature() to v1-d49b18cc81ab79fb. is_po_box, street_key, street_num and the address key all move on the rows above, and is_mail_only and mail_key are new columns, so matchdb must rebuild its derived columns — and should take .md_pobox_pat from np_pattern("pobox") and add the "mailonly" gate in the same change, or its md_place_key() macro will be narrower than np_addr_key() in two separate ways. npmatch needs no change: it reads is_po_box only, for geo_pobox.

R CMD check: Status OK. 216 test assertions pass. # npnormalize 0.1.5

An audit of PO-box detection against the 3,687,435-row unified BMF, the one defect it found that is this package’s to fix, and the first half of a fix for the four packages drifting apart on box patterns. The audit is dev/audit-pobox.R, kept as the record; it reads the raw street line rather than the key, because a spelling can only be judged against what the filer actually wrote.

What detection looks like today

Nothing is being vacuumed up. is_po_box is 579,602 rows (15.718%) in 78,936 distinct keys, and of the 1,000 sampled detections (weighted by row), none lacks a box word on the raw line. Across the whole corpus only 30 rows do, and every one is a box written without a space — PO762, PO25762. By spelling:

what matched rows
PO BOX / P O BOX / POBOX 578,684
a bare BOX 682
PO / P O, no box word 164
POB / PO B 72

The precision edge that does exist is the dual address line: 1,141 rows carry text after the box number, 136 of them a whole street (PO BOX 102175 KOOSER RD), and blanking the address key discards that street. Left as is — it is 0.031% of detections and the alternative is parsing two addresses out of one line.

is_po_box now reads a lettered box

#12. A box identifier is digits or a single letter where the key ends, so PO BOX A through PO BOX Z are boxes:

  • 1,010 rows (0.027%) in 41 keys, 982 of them the PO BOX <letter> alphabet, led by B (119) and A (116). The other 28 are box lines truncated in the filing — PO BO, POB, BOX R. No street in the corpus has a whole key of a designator plus one letter.
  • There is no building at PO BOX Q, but the digits-only pattern meant np_addr_key() kept their keys and counted their holders as a building’s tenants: 105 of their 825 address keys hold two or more EINs, up to 15 at PO BOX B 75785.
  • The anchor sits on the letter branch only. A box number is routinely followed by more text, so anchoring the whole identifier would have dropped the 1,141 rows above; a test asserts the widened pattern still flags every spelling the digits form flagged, and the pattern added 41 keys and lost 0 over the full corpus.

The letter has to survive the rewrite, and a new helper .np_box_identifier() is what makes it: np_normalize()’s "PO BOX <id>" rewrite read [0-9]+, so a widened flag alone would have rewritten PO BOX A and PO BOX B to the same bare PO BOX — two different boxes collapsed onto one address, worse than not flagging them. .np_parse_street() reads the same helper, so the key and street_num always name the same box. That also recovers 236 rows whose box number was NA: the old parse required the literal word BOX, so POB 25161 and PO 1609 lost theirs although the key says PO BOX 25161.

One vocabulary, and a way for other packages to read it

The four packages had drifted. pfmatch kept .PF_BOX_RE, an unanchored BOX that claims 127 BMF rows whose street is merely named for a box (BOX ELDER ST, BOX SPGS RD); matchdb keeps .md_pobox_pat, a hand-typed copy of this package’s pattern, because DuckDB’s R client registers data frames, not scalar UDFs, so a SQL macro cannot call np_addr_key().

  • .np_box_head and .np_box_id are the vocabulary; .np_pobox_pat is composed from them, and .np_unit_id_strip is lifted out of np_unit_id() for the same reason. Only the composed values are in the signature registry — editing a piece still moves the signature, rearranging the pieces does not.
  • np_is_po_box() and np_has_box() answer the two box questions for a caller holding one free-text line, which is what a consumer keeping its own BOX regex actually wanted. np_has_box() no longer depends on the rewrite, so POBOX 12 answers TRUE (there is no word boundary before BOX, so the tail pattern alone cannot see it).
  • np_pattern() hands out the literals — "pobox", "box", "unit_id" — for a consumer that cannot call an R function at all. The patterns are written in the subset R’s own engine and RE2 share, with no lookaround (which R rejects too, without perl = TRUE) and no \d.
  • test-portability.R runs each published pattern through both engines over one fixture and asserts they agree, and asserts the composition. That is what keeps a SQL copy honest rather than merely hand-ported.

Downstream

  • This moves the signature, to v1-533f186c123357cf: is_po_box, street_key, street_num and the address key all move on the rows above, so matchdb must rebuild its derived columns. It should take .md_pobox_pat from np_pattern("pobox") in the same change, or its md_place_key() macro will be narrower than np_addr_key().
  • pfmatch can now replace .PF_BOX_RE with npnormalize::np_has_box().
  • npmatch needs no change: it reads is_po_box only for geo_pobox.

Measured and not changed

  • The bare designator — a key that is PO BOX and nothing else, 460 rows — is still not a box, and np_addr_key() still keys it. #12 suspected this collapsed a ZIP’s boxes onto one address; it does not. Those 460 rows hold 455 address keys, 4 of which have two or more EINs, at most 3.
  • The designator families is_po_box does not see are left for their own issue, with the measurement in dev/audit-pobox.R section C: rural routes carrying a box (RR 1 BOX 8, 4,625 rows), military PSC / APO / FPO (343), GENERAL DELIVERY (164), DRAWER (77), and the long tail of PO BX, BX, PB, POSTAL, APARTADO and BUZON (a dozen rows each or fewer). PMB (13,700 rows) is deliberately not among them: a private mailbox sits at a real street address, which the key keeps.

npnormalize 0.1.4

A new address column asked for in #9, and a defect the measurement for it turned up. Both were measured against the 3,687,435-row unified BMF; the scan is dev/scan-box-component.R, kept as the record, the way scan-unit-designators.R is for the designator list.

  • street_has_box, a second question about a box: does the street carry a box component, whether or not the whole street is one. is_po_box cannot answer it and should not be widened to — it is the gate that blanks the address key in np_addr_key(), so widening it would stop counting records at streets that are genuine buildings. Filers write the street on line 1 ending in the box word and carry the box number alone on line 2, and a consumer holding that bare number had nothing to tell a box number from a door:

    raw street street_key is_po_box street_has_box
    211 EMMET STREET SOUTH PO BOX 211 EMMET ST S PO BOX FALSE TRUE
    300 KENAN CENTER DRIVE - CAMPUS BOX 300 KENAN CENTER DR CAMPUS BOX FALSE TRUE
    ONE HARRISON PLAZA BOX 5079 ONE HARRISON PLAZA BOX 5079 FALSE TRUE
    PO BOX A PO BOX A FALSE TRUE
    PO BOX 1367 PO BOX 1367 TRUE TRUE
    22009 BOX ELDER RD 22009 BOX ELDER RD FALSE FALSE

    is_po_box implies street_has_box on every row, because the flag is read from the key np_normalize() publishes — so a consumer holding a cached street_key can recompute it without re-normalizing.

    The box word has to end the key, with at most digits or a single letter after it. That anchor is the whole guard, and the reason the pattern is not the unanchored BOX pfmatch keeps locally: a bare \bBOX\b matches 2,099 rows the anchored form does not, and 127 of them are streets named for a box (BOX SPGS RD, BOX ELDER ST, BOX RD). The anchored form flags 1 of those 405 rows, and that one is a box. BOXWOOD and BOXER never match either way.

    The flag adds 11,982 rows (0.325%) to the 579,602 is_po_box already reports: 562 a street then a bare BOX, 10,345 a street then BOX <number>, and 1,075 a lettered box (PO BOX A … PO BOX Z, which .np_pobox_pat misses because it requires digits). DRAWER and BIN were measured and left out at 55 and 28 rows, against a false positive already visible at that volume (1206 GRAIN BIN RD).

    street_unit is deliberately not changed by this. The flag says the street has a box, not that a companion number is that box’s — the street can name a suite as well (4347 W NORTHWEST HWY STE 130 BOX), and that call belongs to whoever holds the second line. 0.1.2 already removed the sharp edge by making np_unit_id("400891") NA; this adds the positive signal a consumer can key on, and lets pfmatch replace its local .PF_BOX_RE with a column.

  • .np_parse_street() now treats only an anchored box as a box. Its gate was an unanchored grepl("\\bBOX\\b"), which overwrote the parse of 14,014 BMF rows (0.380%) whose street merely carries or is named for a box, on rows where is_po_box said FALSE:

    street_key 0.1.3 street_num / street_name 0.1.4
    ONE HARRISON PLZ BOX 5079 5079 / PO BOX NA / ONE HARRISON PLZ BOX 5079
    22009 BOX ELDER RD NA / PO BOX 22009 / BOX ELDER (type RD)
    211 EMMET ST S PO BOX NA / PO BOX 211 / EMMET ST S PO BOX
    PO BOX 12 12 / PO BOX 12 / PO BOX

    A BOX-named street used to lose its house number to a box number it does not have, and two records agreed on a street_num neither had. The parse and is_po_box can no longer disagree about what a box is, which a test asserts.

  • This moves the signature, to v1-1179714ce1e9d31f. street_has_box is a new cached column and street_num / street_name move on the rows above, so matchdb must rebuild its derived columns again — the 0.1.3 rebuild (matchdb#29) had already closed, so this does not ride along with it.

  • npmatch needs no change: it reads is_po_box only for geo_pobox, and the new column is additive.

npnormalize 0.1.3

Two parsing rules that 0.1.2 carried further, found when matchdb rebuilt under it (matchdb#29). Neither changes street_key, so blocking is unaffected.

  • A line naming several units keeps the most specific one, not the first one written. Every unit is cut from street_key, but street_unit holds one, and the first was often the one that does not tell occupants apart:

    raw street 0.1.2 street_unit 0.1.3
    1 BETHANY RD BUILDING 1 STE 5 BLDG 1 STE 5
    2125 BISCAYNE BLVD STE 204 # 22915 STE 204 # 22915
    1633 MAIN ST STE A PMB 175 STE A PMB 175
    123 MAIN ST RM 3 FL 2 RM 3 RM 3

    The rank (.np_unit_rank) runs building < floor or area < door < mailbox, and between two of one rank the last wins, because an address is written from the outside in. In matchdb’s 13.0M address strings, 56,466 name two or more units, and the pick changes for 54,936 of them (17,724 current address rows), mostly a mail store’s suite giving way to the customer’s box. The second address line is read by the same rule.

  • The house number is a whole leading token. An ordinal street has none: 16TH ST gave street_num 16T and street_name H, so two such records agreed on a house number neither has. Grid numbers stay whole (16W540 BLUFF RD, which gave 16W), and a number run into the street name is its digits (921AIRPORT SERVICE RD gives 921 on AIRPORT SERVICE, not 921A on IRPORT SERVICE) unless they could begin an ordinal. 19,909 of matchdb’s address strings change.

  • This moves the signature, to v1-592912060053c4c3. Cached street_unit, street_unit_id, street_num and street_name values must be rebuilt.

npnormalize 0.1.2

Two unit-extraction bugs reported from pfmatch, which parses the free-text secondary-unit line of Form 990-PF Part XIV Table 3a with this package (#7).

  • BUILDING is now a unit designator, as its abbreviation BLDG already was. The unit is extracted from the raw street, while .np_street_types contracts BUILDING -> BLDG two lines later in np_normalize(), so the pattern never saw the one spelling it recognized and the two spellings of one address disagreed on both outputs:

    raw street street_key street_unit
    100 CAMPUS CENTER BUILDING 86E was 100 CAMPUS CENTER BLDG 86E was NA
    100 CAMPUS CENTER BLDG 86E 100 CAMPUS CENTER BLDG 86E

    Both now key as 100 CAMPUS CENTER with unit BLDG 86E, so the pair blocks and compares. BUILDING is still an ordinary street word where no identifier follows it (1 EMPIRE STATE BUILDING, 4 BUILDING COMMISSION RD).

    • A test asserts the general case over .np_street_types: every key whose abbreviation is a designator must be a designator itself. This class of bug is invisible one case at a time, because the street key looks right.
    • This moves the signature, to v1-6d90b52d8b781673. Any address spelling the designator out keys differently, so cached keys and the corpus statistics built on them must be rebuilt.

  • np_unit_id() is gated by the designator pattern, so it returns NA for a line that names no unit instead of reducing whatever it was given. It is exported, and a caller handing it a raw address line got confident nonsense with no signal: "PO BOX 1367" gave "BOX1367", "LAS VEGAS" gave "VEGAS", "114 HIGH ST" gave "114HIGHST". All three are now NA.

    • A bare identifier with no designator ("300") is now NA as well, because a digit string alone is as often a box number or a record counter as a door. Pass a dedicated unit column as np_extract_unit()’s unit argument, where a bare value is still accepted.
    • np_normalize() is unaffected: it calls the internal .np_unit_id() on an already-extracted street_unit, and street_unit_id does not change.

  • New exported np_extract_unit(), the single-vector entry point onto that gate: it reads the unit out of one free-text address line exactly as np_normalize() fills street_unit. A consumer parsing one line no longer has to normalize a one-column data frame to reach the gate.

npnormalize 0.1.1

  • New exported np_unit_id(). It reduces a suite as np_normalize() writes it in street_unit ("STE 300", "# 300", "STE D-2") to its identifier ("300", "300", "D2"), which is the street_unit_id column.
    • matchdb’s md_unit_id() needs a public function for this, because it can no longer find npmatch’s internal .np_unit_id() once npmatch imports this package (step 3 of dev/EXTRACTION.md).
    • Like the other four wrappers, it adds nothing of its own, so the signature is unchanged: np_normalize_signature() is still v1-3e7b9f9d59bbb19e.

npnormalize 0.1.0

  • First release. npmatch’s normalizer moved into its own package, every function name and body unchanged (dev/extract-from-npmatch.R, from npmatch@de52bb9):
    • the rule tables;
    • np_normalize(), np_name_core() and np_name_placeholder();
    • the corpus statistics (np_name_freq(), np_token_idf(), np_addr_freq(), np_stopwords());
    • the blocking tokenizer;
    • np_normalize_signature().
  • np_normalize_signature() is v1-3e7b9f9d59bbb19e, as it was in npmatch, and a test pins it.
  • New exported wrappers for the internals npmatch’s matching code calls: np_tokenize(), np_doc_freq(), np_addr_key() and np_state_abb(). They are not part of the signature.
